design_detail: Systematic review and fixed-effect meta-analysis of published randomized placebo-controlled trials in which people who drank alcohol just before or during the trial took repeated usual (therapeutic) doses of acetaminophen (paracetamol) and had serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) measured. Six trials met the criteria; five, with 551 people on acetaminophen and 350 on placebo, reported ALT at one common early time point and were pooled (doses, durations and measurement days in the exposure field). Funded by an investigator-initiated grant from a manufacturer of acetaminophen products. Author manuscript version in PubMed Central.
can_establish: Whether, in the published randomized trials to 2010, mostly of people with heavy drinking who had just stopped drinking in detoxification, a short course of acetaminophen at usual doses raised ALT at an early measurement compared with placebo, and whether any liver failure was reported.
cannot_establish: The risk of rare serious liver injury (with no events among 551 people, the upper 95% limit is about 0.5%; editors' calculation by the rule of three); effects of longer use (ALT rose modestly at later measurements in three trials); effects of taking acetaminophen during a hangover after a single night of heavy drinking (no trial studied that situation); effects of larger doses or of combination products; and whether acetaminophen relieves hangover symptoms (not studied).

sample.recruitment: Searches on 17 November 2010 of MEDLINE (1950 to 2010), EMBASE (1980 to 2010) and International Pharmaceutical Abstracts (1967 to 2009) for acetaminophen terms, with the results filtered for alcohol terms in an internal database, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials to 22 November 2010; no language restriction; published trials only. Four included trials recruited people with heavy drinking admitted to detoxification centres, one moderate drinkers who kept drinking as usual, and one people taking warfarin, most of whom reported light drinking (drinking levels in the exposure field).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized placebo-controlled trials in which participants drank alcohol just before (usually by self-report) or during the trial, took multiple usual doses of acetaminophen (exposure field), and had ALT measured. Of eight randomized trials found, two were excluded because ALT was not measured (Edwards et al., 1982) or not compared between acetaminophen and placebo (Critchley et al., 1983).
sample.demographics: Not tabulated; Table 1 gives each pooled trial's dose, duration and group sizes.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; within trials, Table 2 shows numbers measured falling over time (for example from 306 to 256 in the acetaminophen group of the largest trial).
sample.selection_effects: Published trials only; five of the six included trials and all five pooled trials have authors of this review among their authors (Dart, Green, Heard, Sivilotti), and the earlier systematic review the authors cite (Dart, Kuffner and Rumack, 2000) is also theirs. Mostly people in detoxification who stopped drinking at entry; little information on people who keep drinking.

exposure.measurement: Acetaminophen or placebo given under trial conditions; alcohol use from self-report (no alcohol was allowed during the four detoxification trials).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: 2 to 4 g a day by mouth for 2 to 28 days across the six trials; in the five pooled trials 4 g a day for 2, 3, 5 or 10 days, or 3.9 g a day of a modified-release form for 4 days. In the detoxification trials acetaminophen began within 24 hours of the last drink. ALT was pooled at study day 4 (after the end of dosing in the 2-day and 3-day trials). Later measurements: days 6 and 7 in Dart et al. (one and two days after a 5-day course), day 11 in Heard et al. (one day after a 10-day course), days 14 and 28 in Parra et al. (2 g and 4 g a day). Drinking levels: moderate drinkers in Heard et al. reported 1 to 3 drinks a day; most participants in Parra et al. reported less than 2 oz of alcohol a day.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; one trial was in people taking warfarin.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: In four pooled trials participants were abstinent from alcohol during dosing (the period when, the authors argue, the liver enzyme CYP2E1 is most induced); in one, moderate drinkers continued drinking.

comparison.controls: Placebo groups within each randomized trial.
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials; no formal risk-of-bias assessment of the trials was done.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Nutrition, liver disease and other medicines are not summarized at review level.

outcomes.instruments: Serum ALT; other liver tests (AST, INR, total bilirubin, glutathione S-transferase) summarized narratively; liver dysfunction (bilirubin above 2 mg/dL or INR above 2.0), liver failure and death recorded.
outcomes.validity_norms: ALT is a standard marker of liver-cell injury; the review chose it as the most commonly reported and more specific than AST.
outcomes.operationalization: Primary: the difference between groups in mean change in ALT from baseline at the one early time point reported by most trials (study day in the exposure field); a positive value means a greater rise with acetaminophen.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the single pooled outcome; other time points and tests are reported descriptively.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Two independent abstractors assessed eligibility with a structured form and resolved disagreements by consensus; laboratory outcomes in the trials are objective.

analysis.effect_sizes: Fixed-effect meta-analysis (Comprehensive Meta-Analysis) of five trials at the common early time point: printed as 0.0 IU/L (95% CI −0.2 to 0.1 in the abstract; called a 97% CI in the Results); Q = 1.7, p = 0.8, I2 = 0. The printed values match a standardized difference in means (editors' recalculation from Table 1: −0.04, 95% CI −0.17 to 0.10, Q = 1.6), as the forest-plot legend says, not IU/L; in IU/L the pooled difference is about 0.1 (95% CI −1.3 to 1.5; editors' calculation). Later time points, not pooled: ALT higher with acetaminophen by 12.6 IU/L shortly after the end of a course (Dart et al.), by 8.4 IU/L just after the end of a longer course, statistically significant (Heard et al.), and by 18.7 IU/L at the higher dose and 8.1 IU/L at the lower dose in a trial of people taking warfarin (Parra et al.), with no difference at that trial's last measurement; measurement days in the exposure field. No liver dysfunction, liver failure or death in any trial.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the protocol, analysis methods and inclusion criteria were prespecified but not registered.
analysis.selective_reporting: Planned pooling at several time points was abandoned because trials measured ALT on different days; only one early time point was pooled. Results at other days are shown trial by trial in Table 2.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In five published randomized trials, mostly of people with heavy drinking who had just stopped drinking in detoxification, ALT at the pooled early time point did not rise detectably more with acetaminophen at usual doses than with placebo (pooled difference about 0.1 IU/L, 95% CI about −1.3 to 1.5; editors' calculation), and no trial reported liver failure or death. In two of the five trials acetaminophen had already been stopped before that measurement. Three trials that measured later found modest ALT rises with acetaminophen (about 8 to 19 IU/L) with longer use, mostly just after dosing ended, which had gone at the last measurement of the one trial that looked.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions say there was no elevation of ALT at the pooled time point at the highest usual dose, and the Discussion that concerns about liver injury from therapeutic doses in people with alcohol dependence are "overstated". Gaps: (1) the pooled estimate is printed in IU/L with an interval of −0.2 to 0.1, which is a standardized difference; (2) the Discussion describes the pooled result as the effect of a fixed number of days of use, while two pooled trials had shorter courses that had ended before the measurement; (3) ALT at one early time point in about 900 people cannot show that rare serious liver injury does not happen; (4) the review was funded by an acetaminophen manufacturer, its senior authors had consulted or testified for that manufacturer, the sponsor reviewed the manuscript, and the authors wrote all five pooled trials, with no formal risk-of-bias assessment. The authors do report the later ALT rises and say their meaning is unclear.

timeline.event: Dart, Kuffner and Rumack systematic review of acetaminophen in people with alcohol dependence (pre-1999 literature; two controlled trials), by authors of this review.
Kuffner et al. randomized trial in detoxification patients, pooled here.
Kuffner et al. multicentre trial in detoxification patients and Heard et al. trial in moderate drinkers, pooled here.
Bartels et al. trial in recently abstinent people with alcohol dependence (modified-release form), pooled here.
Dart et al. trial in detoxification patients, pooled here.

replication.where_it_stands: The pooled trials largely come from one research group and one funder, so their agreement is replication within a team rather than independent replication. No trial has studied acetaminophen taken for a hangover after a single night of heavy drinking.

funding.funder: Investigator-initiated grant from McNeil Consumer Healthcare (a manufacturer of acetaminophen products) to Denver Health; K.H. was supported by NIDA award K08DA020573. The sponsor had no stated role in design, analysis or authorship but reviewed the final manuscript.
funding.declared_conflicts: Five authors (K.H., J.G., B.B., D.A., R.D.) are employees of Denver Health, which has clinical, consulting and research contracts with Cumberland Pharmaceuticals (maker of intravenous acetylcysteine), Cadence Pharmaceuticals and McNeil Consumer Healthcare (makers of acetaminophen products). B.H.R. has provided consulting services to McNeil on behalf of Denver Health and testified on behalf of McNeil in litigation in 2010.
funding.affiliations_note: Review authors are authors of all five pooled trials (Dart, Green and Heard of four; Sivilotti of one) and of the earlier systematic review cited in support.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, placebo-controlled trial, independent of manufacturers, in people who drink heavily on single occasions, giving acetaminophen at usual doses for hangover, with repeated liver tests afterwards; and pooling of individual participant data from all trials, published and unpublished, at every measured day with a formal risk-of-bias assessment, alongside large observational data on serious liver injury.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: People who drink; acetaminophen at usual doses; placebo; ALT and liver events.
The protocol was prespecified but not registered, and it did not include a risk-of-bias assessment.
Randomized trials only, justified by the inability of case reports and retrospective series to establish causation or rates.

Four databases including CENTRAL, keywords given, no language restriction, authors of included trials asked about unpublished work; but restricted to published trials without justification, no trial registries or grey literature, no stated reference-list search, and alcohol terms applied only within an internal database of acetaminophen records. Judged as written for publication restrictions, as for item 4 elsewhere (decision p-amstar2-item4).
The same two independent abstractors used a structured abstraction form with consensus for disagreements; the text implies but does not state separately that extraction was done in duplicate.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The two randomized trials excluded at full text are cited with reasons.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Dose, duration, setting and drinking pattern are described; participants' characteristics are not.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The authors state that no specific assessment of bias was performed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported, although several included trials share the review's authors and institution.

A weighted fixed-effect model justified by I2 of 0. Weaknesses: a standardized difference was used although all trials report ALT in IU/L, and it is printed as IU/L; and the pooled measurement fell after the end of dosing in two of the five trials.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias assessment, so no analysis of its impact.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Interpretation rests on the trials being randomized and blinded, without assessment; the conclusion that concerns are overstated does not consider bias, sponsorship or the authors' own trials.

A funnel plot was examined and the Limitations say publication bias cannot be excluded; with five trials the plot cannot show much, despite the Results' statement that the estimate is not subject to publication bias.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Industry funding, institutional contracts and an author's litigation testimony are disclosed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2: no registered protocol; 4: published trials only without justification; 9: no risk-of-bias assessment; 13: interpretation without regard to bias), which gives critically low confidence. The pooled day-4 result itself is simple and checkable from Table 1, and recalculation confirms no detectable ALT rise at the pooled early time point (in IU/L, about 0.1 with a 95% CI of about −1.3 to 1.5). The card may be cited for that short-term laboratory finding in mostly recently abstinent people with heavy drinking, for the modest ALT rises at later measurements, and for zero reported liver failures among 551 people treated; not for the safety of acetaminophen during a hangover after a single heavy night, for the absence of rare serious injury, or for the authors' conclusion that concerns are overstated.

key_findings.finding: 184 unique records yielded eight randomized trials, of which six met all criteria; five reported ALT at a common early time point (551 people on acetaminophen, 350 on placebo) and were pooled; doses, durations and measurement days are in the exposure field. Four trials were in detoxification patients who had just stopped drinking.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Main Results; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Pooled difference in mean change in ALT from baseline at the common early time point (acetaminophen minus placebo): printed as 0.0 IU/L (95% CI −0.2 to 0.1), with Q = 1.7 (p = 0.8) and I2 = 0, fixed-effect model.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Abstract › Main Results; Figure 2 legend
key_findings.note: Editors' recalculation from Table 1: these numbers are a standardized difference (−0.04, 95% CI −0.17 to 0.10), as the Figure 2 legend says; in IU/L the fixed-effect pooled difference is 0.09 (95% CI −1.27 to 1.46). The Results call the interval a 97% CI.

key_findings.finding: Per-trial changes at the pooled time point (acetaminophen against placebo, IU/L): Kuffner 2001, 5.70 against 5.40; Heard 2007, −0.2 against −0.6; Kuffner 2007, −0.3 against 3.6; Bartels 2008, 3.4 against 4.1; Dart 2010, −2.3 against −3.0. In the two Kuffner trials dosing had ended before this measurement (durations in the exposure field).

Later, unpooled time points: ALT was higher with acetaminophen than placebo by 12.6 IU/L shortly after the end of a course (Dart 2010); by 8.4 IU/L just after the end of a longer course, statistically significant (Heard 2007); and by 18.7 IU/L at the higher dose and 8.1 IU/L at the lower dose in a trial of people taking warfarin (Parra 2007), with no difference at that trial's last measurement (measurement days in the exposure field).
key_findings.note: From Table 2 the first of the two later Dart differences is 6.6 IU/L in raw means (5.6 as change from baseline) against 5.5 in the text, and the Parra difference at the higher dose is 18.3 against 18.7 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: No randomized trial, included or excluded, reported liver dysfunction, liver failure or death; AST, INR, bilirubin and glutathione S-transferase changes were similar between groups where reported, except a rise in INR in people taking warfarin.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st, 5th and 7th paragraphs; Abstract › Main Results
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: with no events among 551 people on acetaminophen in the pooled trials, the upper 95% limit for the event rate is about 0.5% (rule of three).

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that recently abstinent heavy drinkers are at maximal theoretical risk (induced CYP2E1, possible glutathione depletion) and that alcohol present at the time of dosing inhibits the toxic pathway; four of the six included trials studied that recently abstinent period.
The search was restricted to published trials; no formal risk-of-bias assessment was done; the funnel plot of five trials could not exclude publication bias.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Results, 6th paragraph; Limitations, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled estimate is printed as 0.0 IU/L with a 95% CI of −0.2 to 0.1 IU/L, but it reproduces as a standardized difference in means (as the forest-plot legend says); in IU/L the interval is about −1.3 to 1.5 (editors' recalculation from Table 1).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Main Results; Results, 4th paragraph; Figure 2 legend; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must not quote the interval as IU/L; the null result stands on either scale.

reporting_issues.issue: The interval is a 95% CI in the abstract and a 97% CI in the Results.

The Discussion describes the pooled result as the effect of a set number of days of acetaminophen, but in two of the five pooled trials the course was shorter and had ended before the pooled measurement (durations in the exposure field).
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled result describes ALT at one early time point after courses of different lengths, not after a fixed period of continuous use.

reporting_issues.issue: Differences quoted in the text do not all match Table 2: 5.5 IU/L for the first of the two later Dart 2010 values (6.6 in raw means, 5.6 as change from baseline) and 18.7 IU/L for Parra 2007 at the higher dose (18.3); in Table 2 the Parra placebo and higher-dose groups have identical baseline values, 37.3 (SD 10.2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small transcription inconsistencies; the later rises should be quoted as about 6 to 19 IU/L.

reporting_issues.issue: The 1st paragraph of the Discussion says daily acetaminophen does not affect the serum at the pooled time point, with the word ALT missing; the first sentence of the Conclusions lacks a verb.

The Limitations say participants in three of the five pooled trials were recruited at detoxification centres; by the Results and Table 1, four of the five pooled trials (Kuffner 2001, Kuffner 2007, Bartels 2008, Dart 2010) were in detoxification patients and one (Heard 2007) in moderate drinkers.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Limitations, 4th paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled evidence is even more concentrated in recently abstinent heavy drinkers than the Limitations suggest.

reporting_issues.issue: The PubMed Central author manuscript is titled differently from the reference record built from Crossref (the published version's title also names the dose range and serum ALT levels).
reporting_issues.consequence: The editor should confirm that the reference record matches the published version; the content read is the accepted manuscript.
